Investor · Founder · Builder

I keep choosing
founders.

A quick story. In undergrad I was on track to be a finance professional, set to crunch numbers in the markets all day. Along the way a friend pitched me a simple idea for a student-discount platform, and I kept overhearing classmates wanting to start their own companies. Heading the entrepreneurship club, I was inspired enough to launch my university's first incubator, now backed by the Government of India.

Then I took the sensible, secure path: structured finance at a large bank, learning the ropes from industry veterans. But I never forgot the energy I felt around founders.

So, against everyone's advice, I joined a seed-stage fintech as a founding team member, right as India's post-COVID digital wave took off and we were backing that growth. Risky bets, but my ability to grow the business while keeping losses tight eventually earned me an investor seat at one of India's larger funds. I've been choosing founders ever since.

Building · Founder

QuickSave

An AI quick-commerce platform using real-time price aggregation and ML to optimise everyday consumer spend in India.

FounderConsumer AILive prototype

Grocery and quick-commerce prices in India swing constantly across platforms. Households overpay simply because comparing in real time is impossible by hand.

QuickSave aggregates live prices across quick-commerce apps and uses ML to route each basket to the cheapest fulfilment: a savings layer that sits on top of the ecosystem.

I've financed early consumer and enterprise ventures ($5.2M+ deployed at GetVantage) and built AI automation professionally at PPRO. QuickSave is where the investor side and the builder side meet, and building it has changed how I read other founders' products.

Watchlist · Startups worth meeting

Two teams I'd bring
to a pipeline meeting

Written the way I'd write an internal note: archetype, what, why now, signal, and the case for backing it. Funding stage is labelled on each, so it's clear at a glance where each company is in its build.

Note 01Physical AI

Adexis

Stage · Pre-seed, angel-backed, amount undisclosed
Archetype
Research lab before it is a company. Incorporated June 2026, a founding team of four, hiring founding engineers at £100k to £225k with real equity.
What
A visuo-tactile foundation model plus the sensor hardware and real-time inference stack to run it on robot hands. The goal is dexterous manipulation by feel rather than by sight. Their own phrase for it is the somatosensory cortex for physical AI.
Why now
4.66M industrial robots are operational worldwide and installations have cleared 500,000 a year four years running, but almost all of that base is position-controlled and vision-guided. Contact-rich manipulation is the part nobody has solved, and it is the part that unlocks the rest.
Signal
The technical founder holds a UCL PhD in learning from heterogeneous data with limited supervision and came out of Wayve. They say they are backed by investors and researchers from Anthropic, ElevenLabs and Google DeepMind, though the names are not public. No priced round filed.
Why back it
Pre-product and pre-revenue, squarely in the AI-meets-physical-world lane. The risk is plain: no demo, no published research, and a team of four. What is being underwritten here is the background, and this is the only stage at which a first cheque is available.
Note 02Science AI

Prometheux ↗

Stage · Seed, $3.8M raised June 2024 (Giant Ventures, 2100, Firestreak)
Archetype
Science-led spinout out of the knowledge graph labs at Oxford and TU Wien. The CEO still guest-lectures on Oxford's Knowledge Graphs course; the CTO holds the PhD in the underlying logic.
What
Deterministic agents at scale. Write business rules once as an ontology, run them against live enterprise data in place, and trace every answer back to the rules and source rows behind it. Same input, same output, every time. Built on Vadalog, a logic-based framework, and served to agents and apps through an MCP server, API, Python SDK and CLI.
Why now
Every enterprise is being asked to put a language model on top of data it cannot explain, and regulated buyers cannot ship a black box. Neurosymbolic reasoning is the version that survives an audit. It runs natively inside Snowflake and Databricks, or on-premise and air-gapped, so the data never has to move.
Signal
In production with hard buyers: Banca d'Italia, Banca Sella, AstraZeneca, Vodafone, Dompé and an unnamed Fortune 500. At Sella it cut credit risk analysis from 17 minutes to 5 seconds. SOC 2 Type II, peer-reviewed research at IJCAI 2025, and Snowflake, Databricks, NVIDIA and AWS in the partner stack.
Why back it
The honest one: this is past a first cheque. It's on the list because it is the sharpest proof in my network that the science-meets-AI thesis has real enterprise buyers, and two years on from seed it is a relationship worth holding before the next round, not after.

Also in the notebook, and deliberately not on the list

I know the go-to-market and engagement teams at Model ML ($87M raised), Ethos (a16z Series A), Round (seed led by Alstin), Attio (Series B), Dust ($40M Series B led by Sequoia), Modal ($4.65B), Gamma ($68M Series B at $2.1B) and Make (acquired by Celonis). Some of those started with me going out to find the team behind a product I rated. Others started the other way round, because I was already evaluating or running the tool inside my own work.

They range from seed to late stage. This is the network I have built and kept warm across stages, and it is usually where the next founder introduction comes from.

Current favourite: Instinct

A personal AI assistant I text or call instead of opening yet another app. It connects to my inbox, calendar and messages, then does the work itself on its own phone and computer: chasing a dropped thread, booking, triaging email. What sold me is that it follows up before I remember to. It is also the clearest wedge I use: no new interface at all, just a conversation.
